userStories.title: Parallel transcoding of one stream across workers
userStories.description: When a job runs below about 1.2x real time, helper jobs on other workers encode later chunks of the same film, so CPU on every node serves one viewer. Deterministic segments let the chunks splice.
acceptanceCriteria: Design reviewed before building (chunk boundaries, slots, cancellation, read-ahead, failover of a helper)
Three worker processes encode one film in chunks; the assembled segments equal a single worker's video byte for byte
hls.js plays through and seeks across chunk boundaries with no stall or discontinuity
A helper killed mid-chunk is replaced and the viewer keeps playing
Helpers never take the last free slot from a new viewer
Measured speedup with 1, 2 and 3 workers in the PR
userStories.notes: The user's idea: use CPU on all nodes rather than relying on a GPU. 'Gotta test sharding streams.' Built 2026-11-08: a job below 1.2x real time (judged after 2 s of output) inserts a helper row for the next free 4-segment chunk within the viewer's lead; helpers are claimed by other workers first and never take a worker's last free slot. A job's ffmpeg runs on across chunk starts until it reaches a chunk another job holds, so a job nobody helps is one ffmpeg. Measured with each worker's ffmpeg pinned to one CPU: 1 worker 16.3 s, 2 workers 10.4 s (1.57x), 3 workers 8.0 s (2.03x). Re-encoded segments from different runs have the same frames and frame times within 1 ms, not the same bytes (x264 stays multi-threaded). A burnt image subtitle gets no helpers (a run that starts mid-film loses the cue showing at its start); JS-071 closes that gap. A failed helper does not fail the viewer's spec and blocks re-helping its chunk for 30 s. Backlog: helpers are a fixed threshold (1.2x), not a measure of spare capacity across the cluster; a helper's chunk that the viewer never reaches is wasted work until the idle kill; per-helper metrics (JS-021 traces should show which chunks were helped and why).

userStories.title: Keep playback and transcodes through a Postgres failover
userStories.description: A CNPG switchover ends every worker's lock connection; today every transcode restarts. Re-lock first, then check the worker's own row: if it is present nobody touched its jobs and they continue. The stream role has the same failure: every playlist, segment and direct-play request reads Postgres (token, source row, viewer), and a database error is answered with a 500 (internal/api/server.go requireAuth, transcode.go, stream.go), which jellyfin-web treats as the end of playback (DOMAINS.md: any answer of 400 or more destroys the player). So a switchover, the most ordinary Kubernetes event, stops every viewer. The stream role must never answer 5xx for a database that is briefly away.
acceptanceCriteria: Postgres goes away and comes back for a worker at least a second before its jobs' leases run out (9 seconds from the last renewal, renewed every 3): every transcode job on every worker goes on, with three workers each running jobs and viewers asking for segments meanwhile; each job's row, worker and ffmpeg process are the same before and after, and no second job is started for its spec

That holds for a re-encode, a copy and a job paused at its lead, and for both shapes of 'away': every connection ended with new ones accepted at once (a switchover seen through a Service), and every connection ended with new ones refused for some seconds (a restart); in both the rows come back as they were and no advisory lock is held

Every worker's jobs survive, not only those of the first worker to lock again: nothing that looks for dead workers as Postgres returns (each worker's quarter-second reap, a PlaybackInfo on an api replica) forgets a live worker that is still taking its lock again

A segment finished while Postgres is away neither ends the job nor is lost: nothing is stored until the check before every store passes again (invariant 37), then the waiting segments are stored and the job goes on
No job ends `failed` because Postgres was away, and no spec is refused for it afterwards (no 'the last attempt failed' at PlaybackInfo or on a segment): a job the outage does cut short is `cancelled`

An outage that outlasts a job's lease: the worker stops that ffmpeg no later than it does today (its first heartbeat after the lease ran out), stores nothing from it afterwards, and the viewer's next segment request starts the job again at the first missing segment and is answered with the segment, not an error

A worker killed while Postgres is away is forgotten once Postgres is back, and another worker continues its job at the first missing segment; the viewer's request waiting on it is answered with the segment

A worker locks again first and only then looks for its own row: finding it gone (another replica took it for dead), it stops every ffmpeg and puts its row back only afterwards; while it does not hold the lock it claims no new job, however long locking again takes

A worker that cannot take its lock again while Postgres still answers its other queries, and that another replica has forgotten, stops its ffmpeg within the 1 second grace, before a replacement's ffmpeg starts, as a worker that lost its lock does today

No job is ever owned by two workers (invariant 25), shown with real processes under contention: over repeated rounds of ending one worker's lock connection, and of ending every worker's at once, while the other workers and a stream replica reap, the old owner's ffmpeg and a replacement's never run at once for one spec (helpers apart), no worker stores a segment after it was forgotten, and each round ends with the job still on its worker or with that worker's ffmpeg gone before the replacement's starts

While Postgres is away, for at least the 90 seconds a segment request may already wait (WaitTimeout), no stream-role request is answered 400 or more because of it; checked for each of the master playlist, the main playlist, the init segment, a stored segment, a segment its job has yet to make, a segment whose job was queued just before the outage (no 503 for a queue wait that passed while Postgres was away), and a direct-play range request, on two stream replicas with several viewers at once: each gets its usual answer and body, at once or when Postgres is back, and so does a request the player abandoned after 10 seconds and asked again

Postgres being away never lets a request in: one whose token belongs to no signed-in device gets no playlist, segment or film byte while it is away, also from a replica that was serving other viewers a moment before, and is answered 401 at the latest when Postgres is back

With Postgres up, whatever a stream replica keeps in memory is short-lived: a signed-out token is refused, and a film whose source row the scan has changed (a replaced file) is served from the new row, by every stream replica no later than 10 seconds after the change, and at once if the build keeps nothing

In jellyfin-web in the e2e tier, Postgres is restarted in the middle of a film playing as an HLS transcode, and the browser asks for at least one segment while it is away (the scenario counts them): the picture goes on past the point it had reached, with no dialog, the same player and no new PlaybackInfo, and no request the browser made, to either role, is answered 400 or more because of the database

The same in the e2e tier for a film that direct plays, with a seek while Postgres is away to a place the browser has not buffered, so that it must ask for a range: the picture plays on from there (once Postgres is back, at the latest), with no dialog, and no request the browser made is answered 400 or more because of the database

userStories.title: Failover follow-ups
userStories.description: Smaller items from the failover reviews.
acceptanceCriteria: Liveness URL: a worker process started with `--liveness-database-url` connects its liveness lock and its lease keeper through that URL and nothing else: Postgres sees at most two connections from it there (one while it has no job, two while it has one), also after the lock is taken again and the keeper reconnects several times, and every other statement of the process (claims, looks, registration, job rows, hints, scans, sweeps, migrations) goes through `JELLYSCALE_DATABASE_URL`; fails today, where the flag stops the start

Liveness URL: without the flag a worker's lock and keeper connect through `JELLYSCALE_DATABASE_URL` exactly as today, and an `api` or `stream` process given the flag starts and opens no connection to it

Liveness URL: a value that is not a Postgres URL stops the start with an error naming the flag, before anything is written to Postgres; one that parses but refuses connections stops nothing (the worker logs why, claims no job, retries as an unreachable lock connection is retried today, and takes jobs once it connects); one behind a transaction-mode pooler is logged as a lock Postgres does not show is logged today, the line naming `--liveness-database-url`

Liveness URL: with it refusing connections to every worker while the main URL answers (three workers, each with a job, viewers asking for segments), an interruption shorter than a lease less a heartbeat leaves every job its row, worker and ffmpeg and forgets no worker; one longer than a lease ends each job `cancelled`, never `failed`, with no spec refused and no job claimed meanwhile, and the next request starts each again at the first segment not stored

Liveness URL: with `JELLYSCALE_DATABASE_URL` behind a real session-mode pooler (PgBouncer in a container on a Docker-assigned port) and the liveness URL direct, with real processes of every role: a film transcodes and its segments are served, a text subtitle is extracted, a library scan and a sweep run, and a worker killed (SIGKILL) mid-job is replaced before its lease, as it stood at the kill, would have run out (a 30 s lease); the only connections from the workers that bypass the pooler are their liveness ones

Liveness URL: docs/running.md (Configuration and the `max_connections` arithmetic), docs/transcoding.md (Connections) and ARCHITECTURE.md (roles table, control-plane ceiling) name the flag, say the liveness URL must be a direct, session-mode connection, say which pooler modes the main URL may then sit behind (session mode at least) and what breaks under a mode they do not allow, and give what N workers then cost Postgres in direct connections (2N)

One reaper: at every cluster size one worker at a time, the reaper, looks for dead workers: with 60 live workers, as with 3, over at least 20 look periods every statement of a worker that reads `pg_locks` or forgets a node comes from one worker and the other workers send none, so the count does not grow with the number of workers (counted on every connection of every worker); fails today, where each worker sends two such statements a look

One reaper: the reaper killed (SIGKILL, real processes, at least three workers) while it holds a job a viewer waits on: exactly one of the others takes the role, also when several try at once, forgets it on today's conditions (its lock found gone in two looks at least the `confirmGap` apart, the new reaper's own lock held in the same snapshot and not lost within the `hold`), and its job is claimed before its lease, as it stood at the kill, would have run out (a 30 s lease); the same when the reaper and another worker are killed together, both forgotten and both jobs taken over

One reaper: the role does not rest with a worker that cannot do it: while the reaper is stopped (SIGSTOP) with its connections standing, while its looks go unanswered (a database delay past the look's bound), and while its own lock has ended within the `hold`, a worker that holds a trusted lock does the forgetting, so a worker killed meanwhile is forgotten and its job claimed before its lease (30 s) would have run out; the stopped or slow reaper is itself not forgotten and its leases are not cut

One reaper: a worker that is not the reaper still learns in time that it was forgotten: with its lock gone while its connection stands, or forgotten while it could not lock again, it finds its row gone within a `lookPeriod` (at once on the hint) and every transcode ffmpeg of it is gone before a replacement's starts; a worker whose lock ended and whose row is there goes on with its jobs

One reaper: a worker of the release before (its row and its lock as today, taking no part in choosing the reaper, reaping by itself) running beside the new ones is never forgotten while it holds its lock and is forgotten on the same conditions when it is killed, and its own reaping forgets no live new worker

One reaper: nothing else about liveness changes: a worker other than the reaper that is killed is forgotten on today's conditions with its jobs' leases cut to the `forgottenLease`, several at once and no live one; the existing kill, stop, outage, lease-keeper and fault-schedule checks (JS-029, JS-066, JS-104, JS-105) pass with their assertions and bounds untouched; after an outage that ended every connection whichever worker is the reaper forgets nobody within the `hold`; a replica (api, stream) still forgets nobody

One reaper: ARCHITECTURE.md rules 4 and 6, DOMAINS 25 and docs/transcoding.md say there is one reaper, how it is chosen and replaced (killed, stopped, slow, its lock lost), and what reaping then costs Postgres at 50 and at 400 workers, in place of the per-worker figures they give today

Subtitle leases: a worker killed (SIGKILL) while it runs `subtitle_jobs` rows has their leases cut when it is forgotten, as its transcode jobs' are: in the statement that deletes its row, each running row of every kind (a film's text pass, a subtitle file beside the film, a `.sup`, fonts, chapter pictures) is left at most the `forgottenLease` from then and never a longer lease than it had; shown with several rows of one worker beside a transcode job, and with two workers forgotten in one look

Subtitle leases: another worker then claims each such row before the lease it had at the kill would have run out (a 30 s lease, so a build that waits the lease out fails), the request that was waiting is answered with its track and no answer of 500 or more, and the file is read by one more ffmpeg run, not two; fails today, where the row waits out its lease

Subtitle leases: what a lost lease costs a row is unchanged: each takeover counts one attempt, a row whose lease is lost on its third claim fails with today's error and is remembered as today, an ordinary ffmpeg failure still fails the row at once, and a worker stopped gracefully still puts its job back in the queue uncounted

Subtitle leases: none is cut for a worker that is not forgotten: one that only lost its lock and took it again (its row there), every worker through a Postgres outage shorter than a lease less a heartbeat, and a worker stopped (SIGSTOP) with its connections standing each keep their rows' leases and finish with the same ffmpeg; a stopped worker's row is taken over only once the lease it last renewed has run out

Subtitle leases: a worker forgotten while it lives (its lock gone with its connection standing, or unable to lock again) ends the ffmpeg of every extraction and chapter job it runs within the `forgottenLease` and before another worker's ffmpeg for the same row starts, moves no cut lease later (bar the one renewal already waiting on the row when the reap commits, as DOMAINS 25 allows a transcode job) and writes nothing to a row another worker has claimed; the interleaving is forced, not waited for

Subtitle leases: DOMAINS 25 and 43 and docs/transcoding.md (which says today that subtitle extractions and chapter pictures keep their 10 second lease, whoever dies) state the new bound for a killed worker and the fallback that stays (the lease, when no connection closes)

Claim and re-lock: a claim sent before the worker's row is found gone and committed after the worker has stopped its jobs, locked again and put its row back takes a job the worker runs: the job is `running` on this worker with an ffmpeg that stores its first segment (or is still `queued`), never written `cancelled` and never left `running` with no ffmpeg of the worker, the viewer waiting on it is served by that same job row with no second job for the spec; the interleaving is forced by holding the claim's statement, so the check fails on every run of today's tree

Claim and re-lock: the bound of that claim is stated and checked: a claim committed before the worker is forgotten is one of its jobs and ends with them (`cancelled`, never `failed`, started again by the viewer's request), and no claim commits while the worker's row is gone

Claim and re-lock: a claim that overlaps only a re-lock (the lock's connection ended and taken again, the row never gone) costs no job: with the lock's connection ended over and over while jobs are queued and claimed (real contention, at least 200 rounds), every queued job is claimed by one worker and runs, none ends `cancelled`, none has two owners, and a worker still claims nothing while it does not hold its lock

Rollback note: docs/running.md's Rolling update says how to roll back across this release's liveness changes: a worker of the release before stops at start on `--liveness-database-url` and takes its lock and renews its leases through `JELLYSCALE_DATABASE_URL`, so the flag is removed and that URL made a direct, session-mode one again before such a worker starts; and it gives the order workers and replicas roll in, up and back, or says that none is needed

Rollback note: it says what a fleet of both releases does meanwhile: workers of the release before each still look for the dead beside the one reaper, no live worker of either release is forgotten and a dead one of either is, a subtitle row of a worker forgotten by an old worker waits out its lease as before, and a worker from before the liveness lock (a row that took no lock) is never forgotten and is taken over at its lease

userStories.title: API and stream replica failover
userStories.description: An api replica killed mid-film loses neither the picture nor the resume position; WebSockets reconnect to any replica. The stream role carries every byte and is in no failure test: kill and roll a stream replica too, for HLS and direct play. On SIGTERM a replica fails readiness first, then drains for a grace that matches the pod's termination grace period.
acceptanceCriteria: e2e, api kill: with two api replicas behind the router, SIGKILL the one holding the viewer's socket (sessions.ws_replica names it) while a film plays: the film plays at least 30 s past the kill on the same player, with no Playback Error dialog, no sign-in page and no new PlaybackInfo

Progress persists through that kill: every Progress and Stopped report the browser sends after it is answered 2xx by the live replica (only a request in flight on the killed replica may fail), and once the viewer stops, the film's resume position is where they stopped, past the position at the kill, and playing it again resumes there

The socket reconnects: after that kill the browser has an open /socket again on a live replica (the survivor, or one started since), which sent it ForceKeepAlive, while the film still plays and without the viewer reloading or signing in

Ownership moves: once a device's socket is open on a live replica, sessions.ws_replica names that replica and never the killed one again, also after the new socket closes (then NULL, or the device's newest socket on another live replica)

A device that does not reconnect: within two minutes of the kill sessions.ws_replica names no killed replica, with no socket of the device having to close first; a device with sockets on two replicas whose newer one was on the killed replica is then owned by the live one
A replica stopped with SIGTERM closes its WebSockets and removes their session_sockets rows before it exits: clients see the close, and from its exit sessions.ws_replica names it for no device

e2e, stream kill, HLS: with two stream replicas behind the router, SIGKILL one that is serving a transcoding film's segments: the film plays past everything the player had buffered at the kill, on segments the other replica serves, on the same player, with no Playback Error dialog and no new PlaybackInfo

e2e, stream kill, direct play: SIGKILL the stream replica that is sending a film still being downloaded: the film plays past everything buffered at the kill, on ranges the other replica serves, with no Playback Error dialog, and stays a direct play (no new PlaybackInfo, no transcode)

e2e, stream roll, HLS and direct play: the same two kinds of film each play past everything buffered when one stream replica gets SIGTERM and a replacement is started; in the HLS case no playlist or segment request fails or is answered 400 or more, and the replacement serves the film once it is ready

Readiness is its own route, answered without a token by api and stream replicas alike: 200 while the replica takes requests; GET /healthz goes on answering 2xx through a drain and through a Postgres outage of any length

On SIGTERM readiness answers 503 from then on, before anything is refused: for a documented time after the first 503 the replica still accepts new requests and answers them normally, so a router that polls readiness loses none

Responses in flight when it stops accepting (a segment waiting on its job, a direct-play range mid-body) are sent whole if they end within the grace, and the process then exits by itself; one that outlasts the grace is cut at its end and the process exits within seconds of it, so a slow or hung client never holds a replica

The grace is one config setting with a documented default: the exit time of a replica with an endless response follows two different values, a value that is not a duration or is negative is refused at start, and docs/running.md says to set the pod's termination grace period above it

Postgres away for less than a switchover: readiness stays 200 (still 200 at 20 s away), requests wait and are answered without an error once it is back, as before; several short outages that add up to more than 30 s never fail readiness

Postgres away continuously for longer (503 by 40 s): readiness fails only on the replicas that cannot reach it, requests already waiting go on waiting as before (a segment up to 90 s), and readiness is 200 again within seconds of Postgres answering, with no restart

SIGTERM while Postgres is away, before or after readiness has failed for it: readiness is 503 at once and the process exits by the end of the grace, though its requests wait on the database and its socket rows cannot be removed

userStories.title: Lease and failover invariant tests under fault injection
userStories.description: Property-style tests with real processes over randomized schedules: kill a worker mid-lease, restart Postgres, pause a worker (SIGSTOP), slow the database; assert at most one owner per job, no job lost, and resumption within the stated bound; a soak mode for flake hunting.
acceptanceCriteria: A schedule is a list of steps drawn from one seed and run against real processes: at least three worker processes, all of one output version (a killed one is replaced by a new process), two stream replicas, and at least three viewers playing forward on at least two specs, two of them playing one spec in step through different replicas

The steps fall in random order and at random moments, alone and overlapping: SIGKILL of a worker that holds a job's lease; a Postgres restart (every connection of every process ended at once and refused until it is back), shorter than a lease less a heartbeat and longer than a lease; SIGSTOP then SIGCONT of a worker, shorter than a lease less a heartbeat, longer than a lease, and longer than the stall limit (`Worker.Stall`); a delay on a worker's database connections, up to a 300 ms round trip and long enough that the check before a put goes unanswered (half a lease); and a Stop of a viewer
Every normal run contains each kind and each length of step at least once, and at least once kills, and at least once stops past its lease, the worker of a job a viewer is waiting on

One worker per job: in every schedule a job's `worker` never changes once it is claimed and no two workers ever run ffmpeg for one job, also when several free workers are woken for one queued job at once; fails with the row lock of the claim (`Worker.claim`) removed

One live job per spec: at no moment do viewers playing a spec in step have more than one job queued or running with an unexpired lease (helpers aside), also when their job dies while both ask through different replicas; fails with the per-spec lock in `Jobs.ensure` removed

No lost job: while a running worker has a free slot (schedules keep one), every viewer that is not stopped is served every segment it asks for, in order, to the end of the schedule, and a job cut short by a step is replaced by one that starts at the first segment not stored, never at the film's start; one request rides out up to three restarts (`maxRestarts`) and schedules stay within that; fails with the waiting request's restart of a dead or cancelled job (`Jobs.segment`) removed

No step fails a job: a job that a kill, a restart, a stop or a delay cuts short ends `cancelled`, never `failed`, and no viewer is answered with a failed job; this includes the job of a worker stopped past both its lease and the stall limit while no viewer waits on it

Resume after a kill: when the worker of a job a viewer waits on is killed while another worker runs with a free slot and Postgres has not been away in the last 10 seconds (`reapHold`), the replacement is claimed before the killed worker's lease, as it stood at the kill, would have run out, under a lease long enough that a build which waits it out cannot pass on a slow machine (30 s in `TestAKilledWorkersJobIsClaimedBeforeItsLeaseRunsOut`); fails with `Reap`'s cut of a dead worker's leases removed

Resume after a stop: a worker stopped while its connections stand is never forgotten and its leases are never cut short; a stop shorter than a lease less a heartbeat leaves its jobs' ids, worker and ffmpeg as they were; after a longer one a job a viewer waits on is taken over only once the lease it last renewed has run out, and the worker, when it continues, stops its own ffmpeg for that job

Resume after a Postgres restart: one shorter than a lease less a heartbeat restarts nothing (every job of a worker not otherwise hit keeps its id, worker and ffmpeg process, no running worker's row is forgotten, and segments finished meanwhile are stored once it is back); one longer than a lease ends those jobs `cancelled`, and the first request after it starts each again at the first segment not stored

A slow database is not a loss: a delay of up to a 300 ms round trip forgets no worker and changes no job's id, worker or ffmpeg; a longer one may end jobs, as `cancelled` only; the one-worker, one-live-job, no-failed-job and dead-owner criteria hold whatever the delay

No segment stored by a dead owner: a worker begins a put only if its last check found the job its own, running, with an unexpired lease and the worker's row present, so no put begins later than that check's round trip (a quarter second, plus any delay the schedule put on that worker) after the job stopped being so; holds for a worker stopped past its lease and continued, one that sat out a restart longer than its lease, and one whose check went unanswered; fails with the check before each put (`Worker.upload`) removed

Each "fails with ... removed" above is shown in the normal mode, not the soak: with that guard removed (or, where another layer hides its removal, the guard the spec names, with the reason) the run fails on that invariant in each of three runs in a row, and replaying one of those runs' printed seeds breaks the same invariant; the report gives the seeds
Each schedule prints its seed and its steps (kind, target, planned moment and length) when it starts, and every failure names the invariant broken, the seed and the step it followed
The steps are a function of the seed alone: built twice from one seed they are the same list, and from another seed a different one; with no seed given, a run draws a new one
One documented environment variable replays a seed: the same steps in the same order with the same targets and lengths; the interleaving of the processes is not replayed, and docs/testing.md says so

The normal run is part of the integration tier with no flag: a fixed number of schedules and steps, not a time budget, a few minutes at most in all, with its durations logged; no bound is judged by a measured duration, only by what the database and the processes recorded (lease and claim times, rows, process ids), so `test/timing-bounds.txt` gains nothing but hang bounds

A soak mode, one environment variable giving the number of repetitions, runs the same tests with a new seed each time and asserts nothing the normal run does not; it prints `passed p of n` with every failing seed and fails if p is less than n; with it unset no test is skipped, and neither `test/integration.sh`, CI nor the build workflow sets it
docs/testing.md gives the soak command and the replay of a seed, and says the soak is for flake hunts and is not a step before merging

A Stop cancels no job of a spec that none of the viewers it stopped was on, whatever that spec's viewer rows say at that moment; shown with real contention over at least 200 rounds (as `TestStopRacingAnInsertLeavesNoJob`): Stops of one viewer racing another viewer's move to a new job after its previous job ended; fails today

On one spec, stopping one of two viewers never cancels the job the other is waiting on or last waited on (DOMAINS 38), also while the other is being moved to a new job after its previous one ended; the other's request is answered by that same job and costs it no restart; same contention, at least 200 rounds

A Stop still cancels at once every job of the stopped viewers' specs that no unstopped viewer is watching, including a job they joined but did not start and a helper when its spec's last viewer stops, so the slot is free for the next job

Under the randomized schedules, where Stops fall beside kills, stops of workers and restarts, no job whose worker is running and whose lease is unexpired is ever cancelled while a viewer that is not stopped is watching it
userStories.notes: Evidence: tests block regressions where review comments do not (Anthropic's C compiler: CI stopped new features breaking old ones; agentic property-based testing found real bugs, 86% valid among top-ranked reports).

Check every response against Jellyfin 12.4's own OpenAPI schema, taken from the Jellyfin container the differential tier already starts, in the differential and e2e tiers; and check that every route the SDK clients call on their main paths answers. Where an SDK can run (the Kotlin SDK, as in ~/.cache/jellyscale/sdkjvm/Decode.java; @jellyfin/sdk), decode our answers with it too.
acceptanceCriteria: The differential tier checks every JSON response jellyscale gives it (each request of test/differential/requests.yaml and the tier's own sign-in and setup calls, stub routes included) against the type Jellyfin 12.4's OpenAPI schema gives that route and status, and fails on any violation

The e2e tier does the same for every JSON response jellyfin-web receives from jellyscale in each of its four gates (browse, play, subtitles, transcode), using the checked-in schema and no Jellyfin container

A violation is: a field the schema requires (however the 12.4 document marks it) that is absent or null, at any depth and in every element of an array, not only the first; a value of another type than the schema's (a string for a number, a fraction for an integer, null where not nullable, a string outside its enum, a malformed uuid or date-time); or no JSON body where the schema gives one. Each fails the differential tier and every e2e gate that receives that response, and the failure names the request or route, the JSON path and the field

With ProductName put back to "jellyscale" (#44) the differential tier fails; it is a wrong value, which no schema catches, so the failure comes from SDK discovery or from comparing GET /System/Info/Public with Jellyfin's answer
No entry in compat/differences.yaml excuses a schema violation: with a #47 field removed and its difference listed there as a gap, the differential tier still fails
The same check run on Jellyfin 12.4's own answers to the differential requests reports no violation, so jellyscale is held to no rule Jellyfin's own answers break

A response is matched to its operation whatever the case of its path and the names of its parameters, and an alias is checked as the route it stands for; a JSON response that matches no operation or no declared type fails the tier unless its route is in a checked-in list with a reason

userStories.title: Burnt image subtitles in every run: helpers, seeks and failovers draw the cue that is showing
userStories.description: A PGS, VobSub or DVB cue is one packet when it appears, so an ffmpeg that begins mid-film (a seek, a failover, a helper's chunk) never sees the cue already on screen and leaves it out until the next one (DOMAINS 51's known departure). JS-024 therefore gives burnt image subtitles no helpers: a slow 4K film with Blu-ray subtitles stalls on one worker as before. PRODUCT.md (The experience we're building) promises that every film gets every capability. Make a run that begins at segment N draw the cue showing at N: start its ffmpeg early enough to read that cue's packet (the packet time comes from the track itself, read once and cached like the PGS file copy) and drop the frames before N, or another way that keeps the segment's frames at a single run's times. Then let burnt image subtitles be chunked and helped like any slow re-encode.
acceptanceCriteria: Every run that begins at a segment N > 0 inside a burnt image cue draws, from its first frame until the cue ends, the picture a run from zero draws there, for each of PGS, VobSub and DVB; shown for a seek, a failover restart and a helper's chunk, each through a worker's job (TestBurnedImageSubtitleIsAtTheRightTime without its known-departure case)

The same holds for a cue that began long before the cut (50 s or more, several chunks back), on a film the scan has read, with the cue times reaching the run as they do in production and never handed in by the test
The same holds for a film whose index the scan does not read today: MPEG-2 video with a VobSub track in Matroska (a DVD rip)

With several cues in the film a run draws only what a run from zero shows at its cut: nothing in the gap after a cue has ended, before the first cue or after the last, and the later cue (not the earlier) when it begins inside the second of two
A PGS picture built by more than one packet (a line added while an earlier line stays on screen) is drawn whole by a run that begins after the later packet, as a run from zero draws it

A run that begins where no cue is showing, 50 s or more after the last cue ended, reads no more bytes of the film before its first segment than the same run without the track (within the spread of repeated runs), for each of PGS (ended by a clear packet), VobSub (ended by its duration) and DVB (whose clear packet carries a duration); measured through a worker's job

A run that begins inside a cue reads, beyond the same run without the track, at most the film from that cue's first packet to the cut; checked for a cue 8 s old and one 50 s old through a worker's job with the cue times as production supplies them, and the bound does not grow with the gap before the cue
A run from segment 0, and a run whose image track is a file beside the film, read nothing they do not read today

No job (from zero, a seek, a failover or a helper) starts or waits on a read of the whole film, or any read that grows with the film's length, to learn cue times: the first mid-film run on a film reads the same before its first segment for the same cue in a film four times as long
Two runs of one film that begin at once on two workers (two helpers, or a helper and a seek) each stay within one run's bound, and neither waits for a read the other makes

If learning the cue times takes a read that fails for a reason that is not the film's (a store error, a timeout, the job ending), the run does not go on as if nothing were showing: no segment is stored without a cue a run from zero draws, the failure is not remembered as the film's, and the read ends with its job

A film that lists no times for the track without a whole-film read (MPEG-TS; a Matroska written without cue points for the track) still starts no whole-film read: a mid-film run reads at most a stated look-back more than the run without the track, shows a cue that began within that look-back from its first frame, and an older cue is the one remaining gap, pinned by a test on both sides of the look-back
A film already in the library when the release is deployed (scanned by the previous release, its file unchanged) meets these criteria by the next scan at the latest, with no step by the operator
After a film's file is replaced by one whose cues fall at other times, a mid-film run draws and reads by the new file's cues, never the old file's

docs/transcoding.md records a seek's bytes read and time to first segment, measured through a worker on a film of stated size and bitrate, for origin/main and for this build: with no cue showing, inside a cue 8 s old and one 50 s old, and for the first mid-film run on a film as well as a later one; no check passes or fails on a duration

A slow re-encode with a burnt image subtitle, inside the film or in a file beside it, gets helpers as the same film without the track does (TestABurntImageSubtitleGetsNoHelpers inverted), with at least one helper's chunk beginning inside a cue and one beginning where nothing is showing

Every segment of that helped run has the same number of video frames at the same times (within 1 ms) as a single worker's run from zero, whichever run made it, and so does every segment a seek or a failover run makes

jellyfin-web plays a slow film with a burnt PGS track across a helper's chunk start that falls inside a cue: the cue is on screen before the chunk start, at the first frame played from the helper's segment and until the cue ends, that segment was made by the helper, and the player reports no error

userStories.title: A new viewer never waits behind a helper
userStories.description: Helper jobs (JS-024) may fill every free transcode slot but one across the cluster and hold it until their chunk is done, so a second viewer who starts at the same moment queues behind them. A viewer's job takes a helper's slot instead: the helper stops, and its chunk falls back to the job that asked for help (or to another helper later). Operators can turn helpers off.
acceptanceCriteria: With every slot but one held by helpers, two new viewers start at the same moment on separate worker processes and both get their first segment as fast as with no helpers running
The preempted helper's chunk is still made: the helped viewer plays through it with no stall beyond what a seek costs
A helper is never preempted by another helper
An operator setting turns helpers off; with it off, a slow job is one ffmpeg and inserts no helper rows; documented in docs/running.md
No preemption ever stops a viewer's own job
userStories.source: JS-024 post-task review (2026-11-08); the user chose to land JS-024 and fix this next
userStories.notes: Found reading the helper slot guard after the build: freeSlots is cluster-wide, so helpers keep one slot free for the whole cluster, not per worker. Priority 2 puts it ahead of JS-025. Built 2026-11-08: a viewer's job, under the cluster-wide helpers lock, cancels one helper when no slot is free (a queued one first, else the one furthest ahead, only on a live worker), then sends a preempt hint after its transaction commits; a running helper beats on that hint, and once as it subscribes, so it gives its slot back at once rather than at its next heartbeat. Measured: with a paused helper, a 10 s heartbeat and the viewer arriving just after the helper beat, the viewer's first segment took 5.75 s, the same as on an idle cluster; without the hint it was refused. transcodeHelpers: false on a worker turns its helpers off. userStories.title: Watch state survives a file missing from one scan, and libraries keep their identity
userStories.description: A scan deletes the item of every file the listing no longer shows, and a user's watch state cascades from the item (internal/library/scan.go, migration 0001 user_item_data ON DELETE CASCADE); a file that returns gets a new id. The only guard is a store that lists no video at all. So one disk of a pooled mount dropping out, a half-finished sync, a file replaced in two steps or an S3 re-upload under a new key loses positions, played flags and favourites for good, and changes ids clients hold. A library's id is a hash of its name, so renaming it in config creates a second library, and a library removed from config is never removed.
acceptanceCriteria: A film or episode whose file a scan no longer lists is hidden, not deleted: its item, its media source and every user's user_item_data row stay in the database unchanged.

While it is hidden a viewer sees what they would if it had been deleted: no listing, search, search hint, Latest, Suggestions, Resume, season list or episode list shows it, no TotalRecordCount counts it, and GET /Items/{id} answers as for an unknown id.

A series or season whose every episode is hidden is hidden with them and keeps its id and its own watch state (a favourite on the series); one with an episode still listed stays and shows only the episodes still there.

A file listed again at its old key inside the grace, unchanged or replaced by new content, is shown again as the same item: same item id, media source id and date added, with every user's row as it was (position, played, favourite, play count, last played) for two or more users, and it is not probed again when its size and ETag are unchanged.
The grace is configurable and its default is days long (at least two days); a value that cannot be read or is negative stops the start with an error naming the key.

The grace runs from the first scan that missed the file and is kept in the database: however many scans run in between, on whichever worker and across worker restarts, none removes a hidden item before the grace has passed, and a file that returns and goes missing again starts a new grace.

The first successful scan after the grace has passed removes the item with its watch state, and then any season or series left with no episode at all, hidden or not; a file that returns after that is a new item.

A file listed under another key of the same library with the same size and ETag as a hidden item, in any later scan inside the grace, takes that item's id and watch state and is named and placed by its new key; a move seen within one scan still does (DOMAINS invariant 5).

The same holds when the bytes are the same but the ETag is not (a POSIX copy with a new modification time, an S3 upload with another part size): the file is matched by its size and the probe's fingerprint.
A new file whose content differs from every hidden item's gets a new item with no watch state, even when its size equals a hidden item's: nothing is matched on size alone.

A hidden item goes to at most one file and a file takes at most one item: two identical files appearing for one hidden item give one old item and one new one, and a copy of a file that is still listed never takes that file's item.

An item whose key is listed is never hidden or removed, and a returning or moved file whose probe fails (the file's fault or the store's) creates no second item and loses no row: the next scan tries again and matches it then.

A scan that would lose more than the set share of a library's stored files fails as the empty-mount guard does: Scan returns an error naming the library, how many files are lost and how many are stored (so the scan is logged as failed and jellyscale_scan_last_success is 0), and it hides nothing and removes nothing, not even a hidden item whose grace has passed.

Lost means absent from the listing and matched to no listed file, files already hidden included: a library whose every file moved in one scan passes the guard and keeps every id, a loss of exactly the share passes (the files are hidden), one file more trips it, and two scans each under the share but together over it trip it on the second.
The first scan after the files are back succeeds with every item id and every user_item_data row as before the loss, and a tripped guard in one library changes nothing in another library's scan.
The empty-mount guard (a store that lists no video) and a listing that fails (store error, timeout, cancelled scan) still hide nothing and remove nothing.

A library stored before this change keeps the id it has today (the hash of its name) when the server starts with the same config, and replicas that start at the same instant with one config leave one row per library and agree on its id.

A config that changes only a library's name leaves one library with the same id and the new name in /UserViews, every item id and user_item_data row unchanged, the other libraries untouched and nothing removed when the grace later passes; twelve replicas starting at once with the renamed config still leave one row, and a new library that then takes the old name is a second library with an id of its own.

A library left out of config is hidden, not deleted: /UserViews and GET /Items/{its id} no longer show it and its items are hidden as a missing file's are; put back in config inside the grace it returns with its id, items and every user's watch state.

A library left out of config is removed, with its items and their watch state, only once the grace has passed since the first start without it, never earlier, whichever replica or restart comes in between.

docs/running.md states the grace's key and default, the share and what the operator sees when the guard trips, what to do after removing that many files on purpose, what identifies a library across a rename, and when a library left out of config is removed together with its watch state.

Each case above has a test that seeds user_item_data rows for at least two users (position, played, favourite, and a favourite on a series) and asserts the same rows, by count and content, afterwards; the only tests in which a row goes are the removals after the grace.

Only the worker uses the synced libraries, yet an api or stream replica, or a worker, started with a different or empty libraries list hides every other library from every viewer until a replica with the full config starts again, and removes it after missingGrace. acceptanceCriteria: A process without the worker role (`api`, `stream` or `api,stream`) writes nothing to the libraries at start, whatever its config lists: it adds no library, renames none, changes no store or `chapterImages`, hides none and shows none again.

That holds for each list such a replica may have: no config file, no `libraries` key, an empty list, a subset of the worker's list, an entry under another name for a store the worker lists, and an entry the database lacks.

docs/running.md says that the `libraries` of api and stream replicas are not read, that a worker listing none hides and removes nothing (so emptying the list does not remove the last library), and that a library's grace runs from the first worker start without it, no longer from any start.

userStories.title: Stream segments to the viewer without holding them whole in memory
userStories.description: The stream role reads every segment whole into memory before sending it (internal/transcode/jobs.go readSegment, io.ReadAll). A copied segment carries the file's bitrate and lasts up to 12 seconds (DOMAINS 47), so a 4K copy segment is tens of MB per request, times every concurrent viewer, and a stream pod's memory limit must be set to survive that. Send stored segments as they are read, keeping the guarantee that a cut or empty object is treated as not there yet.
acceptanceCriteria: A stored segment, init or media, is sent while it is read, on the segment route and on the offline path (segmentOffline), from a store with a local path and from one without (S3): the viewer holds the segment's first bytes while the store has not yet given the rest, and receives the object's bytes unchanged

An absent or zero-length object is not there yet: the segment route goes on waiting and asks again, the offline path leaves the request to wait for Postgres as today, and neither ever answers 200 with an empty body
A body that ends early mid-segment and that a reopen at that offset completes (DOMAINS 42), at several offsets of one segment, is sent whole and byte-identical under its Content-Length, with no abort

A segment cut short is never sent with a clean end: if nothing of the response was sent the request waits and reads it again, and if some was the response is aborted, and a later request for that segment is served whole once the object is whole

A store failure that is not 'not found' (Stat or Open: an error, a timeout) before anything is sent ends the request with an error as today, on the offline path leaves it to wait for Postgres, and starts no job; it is never taken for a segment that is not there yet

Every 200 segment response, init or media, on both paths, carries Content-Length equal to the stored object's size and exactly that many bytes; checked with a segment larger than 2048 bytes, since net/http adds the header to a smaller body by itself

An object that gives fewer bytes than the size read for it (truncated after the size was read and still short after the Reader's resumes, or a read that fails mid-body) aborts the response on both paths: the client's read ends in an error after fewer than Content-Length bytes, never a clean end and never padding

An object replaced by one of another size after its size was read is never sent as the new object's bytes cut to the old length, nor ended cleanly short: the response is aborted, or is one object whole under its own length

Every object opened for a segment response is closed when the response ends, whether complete, aborted or left by the viewer mid-segment, and a viewer who leaves mid-segment ends the read from the store

A test holds at least 16 viewers mid-segment at the same moment (each has received part of its segment and stopped reading) on copy segments of at least 16 MiB each, through the stream role's segment route and a store without a local path, and fails unless the process's peak heap growth is under the viewers times a stated per-viewer bound; the bound is at most a sixteenth of the segment and does not grow with the segment's size, so a build that holds segments whole, or reads ahead of a slow viewer without limit, fails it

docs/running.md gives the stream role's memory as a fixed base plus a figure per concurrent viewer, for JS-056's requests and limits, says the figure does not grow with the film's bitrate or the segment's length, and a test fails when the figure differs from the bound the memory test asserts

The store has Stat on both backends, in the conformance suite on POSIX, SeaweedFS and Garage: it returns an object's size without transferring its body, store.ErrNotFound for a missing key, 0 for an empty object, the new size after a replace, and refuses a key that leaves the root
A segment already in the store costs at most one Stat and one Open of the store when no body is cut, and the offline path still asks Postgres nothing

A request waiting for a segment not yet made makes no store request of any kind (Stat, Open, List) after its first look, counted over a wait of at least 5 seconds (20 of today's 250 ms polls) during which at least three other segments of the same spec are stored and hinted; it asks the store again only when a job row or a hint says its segment is stored, or once when the job it waits on is done, cancelled or has lost its lease, as today

A waiting request is answered once its segment is stored and recorded, whichever job of the spec stored it (the one it waits on, another viewer's, a helper's), for several waiters of one segment at once and for waiters on two stream replicas; with every hint lost it is still answered, from the poll of Postgres (DOMAINS 10)

userStories.title: Replace wall-clock ratio bars in tests with checks of the mechanism
userStories.description: Tests that pass or fail on a timing ratio are the largest class of merge-queue escapes (.results escape records for JS-067, JS-024 and JS-072): they pass on a 16-core developer machine and fail on shared CI runners. Convert the existing ratio bars (internal/transcode/helpers_integration_test.go and others found by grep) to checks of what the code does, such as how many helpers ran or which segments each made.
acceptanceCriteria: A timing bar is any assertion a slower runner can fail on a right build: a measured duration with an upper bound, two measured durations compared, or a measured speed with a lower bound or a not-slow flag. None is left in the Go tiers, test/e2e or test/roles.sh, and every assertion the grep finds that compares a measured time or speed is accounted for as replaced or as a hang bound, with the reason.

At least these are bars and are replaced. internal/transcode: helpers_integration_test.go (63 s for three workers; the 60/80/90% bars of TestMoreWorkersFinishTheFilmSooner; the 9 s slowest wait after a killed helper; the 9 s seek into a helper's chunk), helpers_preempt_integration_test.go (9 s slowest wait), hdrcopy_media_integration_test.go (10x real time), failover_integration_test.go (7 s from SIGKILL to the replacement's first segment), chapter_jobs_integration_test.go (2 s subtitle), metrics_integration_test.go (speed 0.6 to 1.5, twice). internal/api: transcoding_info_integration_test.go (EncodeSpeed 0.1 to 0.6 and 1.5 to 6, not flagged at 3x, not below 1 while paused). test/e2e/transcode.mjs: 78 s to reach 60 s of film, and the 5 s and 6 s stand-stills.

Each replacement passes on the unchanged application code and fails on a faulty copy of it with that mechanism removed: one faulty copy for each mechanism named below, each failed by the new check alone and not by a clock, none committed.
Each replacement gives the same verdict on a slow runner: it passes with the test, its workers and their ffmpeg held to two CPUs, and no case is dropped or failed for the number of cores.
No test is deleted, and each test that held a bar keeps every assertion it made that reads no clock.

Workers sharing a slow film, checked with two workers and with three: every worker made segments, no segment was made by two jobs, and jobs on different workers were running at the same moment. It fails when no helper starts, and when the workers make their chunks one after another.

The 4K HDR10 copy with TrueHD: the run decoded and encoded no video frame, and ffmpeg was given the arguments that keep the TrueHD's decoding off the video's path. It fails on a copy that decodes or re-encodes the picture, and on one that decodes the audio in the video's path.

A killed worker's job: the replacement was claimed by the other worker before the dead worker's own lease would have run out, and every request of the viewer was answered. It fails on a build that waits the lease out.

A helper that is killed, a helper stopped for another viewer, and a seek into a helper's chunk: the check is which job made each segment of that chunk (a replacement on another worker from the first segment missing; the viewer's own job after a preemption; the helper itself on a seek, with no job started) and that no request of the viewer failed. Each fails on a build where that job does not make them.

A subtitle asked for while chapter pictures fill their slots: it was read while that many chapter jobs were still running and none had finished since it was asked for. It fails on a build where chapter pictures may take every slot.

A shown speed (EncodeSpeed and Framerate in TranscodingInfo on both replicas, jellyscale_transcode_job_speed_ratio) is checked against what the worker recorded for the job, and against itself across a pause at the lead (not lower after than before); IsBelowRealTime is checked against that speed for one job the test keeps below 1 and one it keeps above. No check needs the runner to encode faster than the film.

In test/e2e/transcode.mjs the parallel and failover scenarios judge by what happened: a helper on another worker made segments past the seam that the player then played, the surviving worker took the job over, no request failed or was abandoned, no error dialog showed, and the buffer has no gap at the seam.

Every timing a bar measured is still measured and logged with what it is (the speedup of two and three workers over one, the copy's multiple of real time, kill to first segment, slowest wait, time to reach 60 s, longest stand-still); no test passes, fails or branches on one.

A time bound stays only where it stops a hang: a wait for an event with a timeout (waitFor, a context deadline, a select on time.After), or a measured bound of at least ten times what a right build takes at that step whose wrong build never delivers, or not before a timer or sleep the test set. A bound closer than that is a bar.
The change touches only test files, test scripts and docs: no file the server or a worker is built from.

docs/testing.md says that tests check mechanisms, not speeds, gives the rule for a time bound that may stay, and names where a run's logged timings are kept; what it says holds for a run that passed, locally and in CI.

userStories.title: A worker claims only specs it can make
userStories.description: Every dogfood deploy is a mixed-version cluster for a while: an older worker can claim a newer spec and store segments made the old way under the new hash, served for 24 h. Put the output version on the job row and in the worker's claim predicate, so an old worker leaves a new spec queued for a new one. Split out of JS-079, which keeps the rest.
acceptanceCriteria: Every transcode job row records an output version: a viewer's job the OutputVersion of the stream or api replica that queued it, a helper the version of the job it helps.
A worker claims a queued job, helper or not, only if the row's version is one the worker makes; a job of another version is never run by it, neither while it is queued nor after it has expired.

A queued job of another version does not hold up a worker: with one or with several such jobs ahead of it in the queue, a job of the worker's own version is claimed at once, not when the others expire.

Shown with real processes on one Postgres and one transcode store, using two builds of the binary that are the same source with OutputVersion changed (the server gains no flag, environment variable or config key for it): with a replica and a worker of each build running at once, viewers on both replicas get their segments, and every job row's version is that of the replica that queued it and of the worker that ran it.

A slow job's helper is made by a worker of the job's version or by none: an idle worker of another version beside it makes no segment of the spec, and in a cluster of one version a helper still starts on another worker.

A viewer's job that no worker of its version takes, while a worker of another version runs with a free slot, waits queueTimeout (6 s) and no less: the segment request is then answered 503 with Retry-After as an untaken job's is today, the row ends cancelled with no worker, and no object is stored under its hash.
A worker of the job's version that starts within queueTimeout claims the waiting job, and the same request is answered with the segment.
The server log line for that 503 names the cause: it does not say that every slot was busy or that no worker runs when a worker of another version had a free slot.

A job queued by a replica built before this release, which writes no version, is still inserted after the migration and counts as version 4, the last output version before rows recorded one: a worker that makes 4 claims it and a worker of a later version does not.

docs/running.md gives, for workers, stream and api, the order to upgrade and the order to roll back in which every version a running replica queues has a running worker that makes it at each step, and keeps its rule that stream is replaced before api.

docs/running.md says what viewers get when that order is not kept (the 503 after queueTimeout, never segments made by another version), and that a worker built before this release makes no such check, so every such worker must be stopped before a replica of a later output version starts.
Walking the documented upgrade order with the two builds as real processes, a viewer who starts playback at each step gets a segment and not a 503, and each job is run by a worker of its version.

DOMAINS.md states the rule the guarantee rests on, that a release whose workers make any spec differently (a new spec field included) bumps OutputVersion, and ARCHITECTURE.md's known departure and docs/status.md's upgrades line say what is now true.

After JS-066's fault injection exists, rewrite keepRow as states (locked, relocking, row gone) with each timing derived from the lease in one table, and cut DOMAINS 25 to that table. Keep the measured 4 s takeover.
acceptanceCriteria: Worker liveness (keepRow and what Present does around it, internal/transcode/liveness.go) is one state machine: its states are named in code (at least locked, relocking and row gone; registration, the lock held and the row not yet inserted, is a named state or a named transition), every transition is named with its event, and the next state for a state and an event is decided in one place that the unit tier can ask with no Postgres.

The transitions are today's and no others: locked to relocking when the lock's connection ends; relocking to locked only once the lock is held again and the row is found there; locked or relocking to row gone when a look finds the row gone; locked to row gone when a look finds the worker's own lock missing from pg_locks while its connection stands; row gone to a new registration only after no job of the old session runs (waited for at most today's 10 s) and a new lock is held; any state to stopped on shutdown.

What each state allows is today's: only a locked worker claims jobs, forgets other workers and refreshes seen_at; a relocking worker's jobs go on with the same ffmpeg processes while it only reads its own row and retries the lock; entering row gone stops every transcode ffmpeg of the worker at once and those jobs end cancelled (interrupted), never failed; the row is inserted once per lock and never put back while relocking.

A look or a registration that Postgres does not answer within its bound is no event in any state: nothing is stopped, nobody is forgotten, and it is tried again at the next look; a worker still registers over a database that takes 300 ms a round trip.

A look runs every look period and also at once, not at the next tick, on each of: the lock's connection ending, a forgot hint for this worker, and the moment a node first seen lockless has been so for the confirmation gap.

A locked worker forgets another only when all three of today's conditions hold (the node's lock gone in two of its looks at least the confirmation gap apart, its own lock held in the same snapshot, its own lock not ended within the hold), for one dead worker and for several at once; a relocking worker and a replica forget nobody and delete no row.

A worker holds at most one liveness connection and runs at most one relock loop at any time, however often its lock connection is ended; after Present returns from any state, mid-relock included, its row is deleted and it holds no liveness lock or connection.

One table in code names every worker-liveness timing, each written as an expression of the default lease and not as a duration of its own; at the 10 s lease each has exactly today's value, no longer and no shorter: lease 10 s, heartbeat and seen_at refresh 3 s, worker counted if seen within 10 s, grace (also the longest a refusal waits on a lockless worker) 1 s, lease left to a forgotten worker's jobs 0.5 s, confirmation gap 0.5 s, bound of a look, row check or refresh 0.5 s, look period 0.25 s, relock retry 50 ms, hold after the worker's own lock ended 10 s.

No duration that decides when a worker looks, retries, gives up a wait, is forgotten or stops counting is written outside that table: none in liveness.go, not the wait in Unavailable or workerAlive in jobs.go, not the 3 s that cmd/jellyscale/main.go passes to Present.

The table is the cluster's, not a worker's: a worker run with another Lease (the tests use 3 s, 20 s, 30 s and 1 min) changes only its jobs' lease, as today, and its liveness timings, Reap's and a replica's stay those of the table at the default lease.

DOMAINS 25 holds the same table as the code, row for row with the same name, the same derivation from the lease and the same value at 10 s, and the states with their transitions; a check fails when a row, derivation or value is changed in the code or in DOMAINS.md alone.

DOMAINS 25 is shorter than today's 811 words, and DOMAINS.md still states every guarantee invariant 25 states today: every job has a kill path and no ffmpeg outlives its lease; losing the lock is not losing the lease; the three conditions for forgetting; a replica forgets nobody; a worker without its row claims, renews and stores nothing; one row per lock; no replacement starts while the old ffmpeg runs, with its stated bound on a slow database; a worker killed during an outage is forgotten up to the hold later; a job ended because Postgres was away is cancelled, never failed; a worker that only lost its lock lets a subtitle extraction finish.

Every existing liveness test (internal/transcode: liveness_test.go, failover_integration_test.go, outage_integration_test.go, idle_replica_outage_integration_test.go, segment_wait_outage_integration_test.go, TestAKilledWorkersJobIsClaimedBeforeItsLeaseRunsOut, TestAWorkerReapedByItsOwnLookIsCounted) and every JS-066 test (faultplan_test.go, faults_integration_test.go, faults_docs_test.go, stop_scope_integration_test.go, claim_race_integration_test.go, stopped_past_stall_integration_test.go) passes with the test process, its worker processes and their ffmpeg held to two CPUs, and the unit tier passes.
None of those tests is deleted, skipped or loosened: each keeps every assertion and every bound it has today, and changes at most the name of a constant or function the rewrite renamed.

Takeover is no slower, shown by mechanism and never by a measured duration: with a second worker free, a SIGKILLed worker's job is claimed by the other before the dead worker's own lease runs out (at leases of 10 s and 30 s), Reap leaves a forgotten worker's running jobs at most the table's 0.5 s of lease, and the time from the kill to the claim is logged, not asserted.

Refusal is no slower: with the last worker killed, a replica's Unavailable waits on the lockless worker no longer than the table's 1 s grace before it answers that no transcode worker is running, deletes no row, and answers without that wait when no counted worker is lockless.

Liveness costs Postgres no more than today: one liveness connection per worker; a locked worker's look is at most two round trips that write nothing unless a node is forgotten, plus the seen_at refresh once per heartbeat; a relocking worker's look is one read of its own row.

The operator's log is today's: the messages liveness.go logs now for the lock's connection ending, a lock Postgres does not show (naming the transaction-mode pooler), being forgotten by another replica, and holding the lock again are logged at the same transitions, once per transition.

userStories.title: Two transcode integration flakes: a test that forgot live workers, and a segment stored after its lease ran out
userStories.description: Two intermittent internal/transcode failures on main failed unrelated PRs' merge-queue runs (2026-11-14): TestEveryJobOfEveryWorkerGoesOnThroughAnOutage/restart, where the test's own reaping loop called the exported Reap and forgot live workers, and a fault schedule in which a worker began a put 3.5 s after its job's lease ran out because the upload did not fence the put against the lease.
acceptanceCriteria: Failure 1 (TestEveryJobOfEveryWorkerGoesOnThroughAnOutage/restart, queue run 43587752815): the cause is recorded with the run or trace that shows it, naming which process deleted the two workers' transcode_nodes rows and at what moment of the outage; or 30 repetitions of that test under 4 CPUs with other load all pass and the cause is argued from the queue run's log.

That record rules each named suspect in or out with evidence, not by reading alone: the frozen-worker rule in worker.go, the reap logic in liveness.go (a worker's own look, and a reap asked for by a process that holds no lock), and a job paused at its lead whose beat is delayed.

Failure 2 (TestFaultSchedulesHoldTheLeaseAndFailoverInvariants, seed 15803960744879474315 schedule 1, queue run 43590049982): the cause is recorded with the run or trace that shows it, naming which step let the put begin (the stop-past-lease SIGSTOP of the worker, or the delay-past-half-lease round trip) and where between asking and storing the lease ran out; or 30 replays of that seed under 4 CPUs with other load all pass and the cause is argued from the queue run's log.
Each cause is fixed in product code; no existing assertion is removed or loosened, no allowance widened, and no retry or skip added to make a test pass.
Each fix has a test that forces the interleaving rather than waiting for it, so it fails on every run of today's tree and passes with the fix.

A worker begins no put for a job after that job's lease ran out when the database answers its ownership check late: asked while the lease stood, answered after it ran out, with a round trip inside the check's own timeout (half a lease) as well as beyond it.

A worker begins no put for a job after that job's lease ran out when the worker itself is late: stopped (SIGSTOP) after it asked and before it stored, for longer than the lease had left, then continued; the first put it could begin after continuing counts.

Both hold for every put of the upload, not only the first: the init segment stored with a job's first segment, and each of several finished segments waiting in scratch; measured against lease_expires_at as Postgres has it, within the fault test's existing 350 ms allowance, which grows neither with the round trip nor with the length of the stop.
The job a worker gives up this way ends cancelled, never failed: PlaybackInfo does not refuse the spec, and the viewer's next request starts a replacement at the first segment not stored.

A Postgres outage that ends every process's connections and is over, for each worker, before its jobs' leases run out forgets no live worker: no worker's transcode_nodes row is missing at any moment, in each shape (switchover, restart with connections refused, terminated by the server), with three workers returning at different times and however long after the first one returned.

Through such an outage every job is the same row on the same worker, still running, with the same ffmpeg process (pid and start time), for a re-encode, a copy and a re-encode paused at its lead alike; each spec has one job, none is cancelled or failed, and the viewers' next segments are served.

That holds when the connections end one after another rather than in one instant (within 0.5 s of each other): a process still connected after other workers' locks are gone, whether a worker holding its lock or a replica holding none that has not yet noticed the outage, forgets nobody and cuts no lease when it reaps in that moment, including when its own connection ends before the answer reaches it.

A worker that is really dead is forgotten as before: killed while Postgres is up, its row is gone and its jobs' leases cut after two looks 0.5 s apart by a live worker; killed during an outage, within reapHold (10 s) of the outage.

A worker that is in time stores as before: a put whose check is answered within the lease goes on, a 50 ms round trip changes nothing, and after a stop shorter than a lease less a heartbeat the job goes on with the same ffmpeg.

userStories.title: One lease keeper for every leased job, so a hung call cannot keep a job past its lease
userStories.description: Worker.encode keeps the lease on the goroutine that does the I/O: the heartbeat, the store puts and most queries share one select loop, and only the ownership check has a deadline (the pool sets no statement timeout, the S3 client uses the SDK's default HTTP client). A query that never answers blocks the loop and the lease check never runs, holding the ffmpeg and the slot. runSubtitle already solves this with a timer that a bounded renewal puts off; lease renewal is written three times with three behaviours (encode, awaitJob, runSubtitle).
acceptanceCriteria: A lease keeper with a connection of its own renews every leased job of the worker, one statement per job table in its own transaction, no keeper statement waits for a row while it holds one, bounded by half a heartbeat, retried at once and then at a short interval when it fails; the transcode loop, awaitJob and runSubtitle use it, and one renewal UPDATE per job table is left in the code

Each job is cut the table's cutMargin (0.5 s) before its lease could lapse, counted from the send of its last confirmed renewal: with the worker's connections held open and unanswered while a job is paused at its lead, its ffmpeg is gone within one lease; with only the pool held and the keeper answering, a job whose work has not come round for a lease is given up, its ffmpeg gone and a replacement serving the next request; a setup copy that is slow but moving counts as work coming round

With every round trip held 1 s (under half a heartbeat), set before the job is claimed, the job goes on and stores every segment; with the keeper's connection alone severed once under that delay, the job goes on; with Postgres away from 2.9 s after a renewal for 3.3 s, every job keeps its row, worker and ffmpeg

No put begins more than a round trip after the job stopped being the worker's, whatever stopped it: a cancel just after a renewal (no put more than 350 ms later), a reap that deletes the row and cuts the lease while the pool is held, a lease held past by a late answer, a worker stopped after the answer; a fence renews only the jobs that asked; the existing fenced-put and outage checks pass

A renewal counts only when confirmed: with the subtitle table's renewal made to fail or block past its bound, the transcode job's lease in Postgres and the keeper's cut agree and the transcode job goes on; under real contention (a worker with two jobs against repeated reaps and cancels, 200 rounds) no request fails and no renewal is lost

The liveness lock's connection refused for longer than a lease while the keeper's and the pool's answer: the worker is not forgotten and the job goes on with the same ffmpeg; the docs state two connections per worker

A Postgres outage that ends 1.5 s before a job's lease can lapse, and a worker stopped until then, cost no job: the same row, worker and ffmpeg, the lease moved on and no job given up (the cut is the lease less the cutMargin, never a heartbeat before it); an outage whose last retry would only come at the next heartbeat still renews by its first retry
userStories.notes: Design reviewed by Fable 5.2 (.results/js105-design-review-2026-11-14.md): the keeper's own connection and batched renewal kept; the put fence still asks Postgres, through the keeper, for the asking jobs only.
