userStories.title: Failed sign-ins are bounded, per name and per address
userStories.description: Nothing bounds failed sign-ins today (the user policy reports LoginAttemptsBeforeLockout -1). D-016 opens the API to any origin, so on a private-network server a web page in a viewer's browser could guess names and passwords and read the answers; servers on the internet are exposed to guessing already.
acceptanceCriteria: Observed first: what Jellyfin 12.4 does after failed sign-ins (its LoginAttemptsBeforeLockout, what a locked account answers) and what jellyfin-web shows for 401, 403, 429 and 503 on sign-in, recorded in compat/captures

Per name (D-020): after 20 failed sign-ins for one name within 15 minutes, from devices that have not signed in to that account before, any number of addresses and replicas, further such sign-ins for it are refused for 15 minutes; a refused attempt checks no password and counts as no failure; a right password during the refusal is refused the same way, and signs in afterwards; no success resets a count and no account is ever disabled by failures; shown with real processes

Known devices (D-020): a device (DeviceId) that held a token for the account within the last 30 days is outside the per-name bound and has its own count for that account, 10 failures within 15 minutes then refused for 15 minutes; with the name refused to strangers under guessing from many addresses, its owner signs in from such a device at the first try, shown by a test; a guesser sending that DeviceId gets no more than that device's count

Per address (D-020, D-022): with proxies declared or `trustedProxies: []`, 10 failed sign-ins within 15 minutes from one address across all names refuse that address for 15 minutes, whatever the name or device, and a success on one account resets nothing; an IPv6 address counts as its /64; one address alone never causes a name to be refused to others, shown by a test (10 failures on one name from one address, then its owner signs in from another address on a new device). The address of a request from a declared proxy is the rightmost X-Forwarded-For entry that is not a declared proxy, and no other entry: when the header is missing, every entry is a declared proxy, or that entry does not parse, the per-address bound is not applied to that request (it neither counts nor is refused per address; the per-name and known-device bounds apply), and a declared proxy's own address is never counted or refused, shown by a test (11 failed sign-ins through a declared proxy with no usable entry, then a right password by the same path signs in). A client behind a declared proxy that appends to the header cannot get itself uncounted or counted as another address by anything it sends (no header, an unparseable one, one naming the proxy's address or another client's), shown by a test
A viewer who mistypes 9 times in a row and then types the right password signs in; every route that takes a password is bounded the same way
The bounds hold under parallel attempts: 200 sign-ins at once for one name, spread over two api replicas, check no more than 20 passwords; shown with two replicas as separate processes

A refusal answers 403 with a Retry-After header in whole seconds until it ends, readable by a cross-origin page (D-016, D-020); it is the same status, body and headers for a name that exists and one that does not (D-014), and an unknown name counts toward the per-name bound exactly as a real one

Unknown names are remembered within a fixed bound stated in docs/access.md; a flood of invented names (100,000 in a test) neither changes nor drops a real account's count, nor makes any unknown name answer differently from a real one at the same count (D-020)

Before any bound, a wrong password and an unknown name answer alike and do the same password work, so the time taken does not tell them apart; shown by a check that can fail (Jellyfin 12.4 was observed at 1 ms against 77 ms)

userStories.title: A segment cut short because its input ended early is never stored, however the worker's upload check and ffmpeg's exit are ordered
userStories.description: Read from two merge-queue runs on 2026-11-20 (JS-155's record, not reproduced): a job whose source read was cut for good failed, yet its request was answered with a segment and no error. As read, the worker's periodic upload check can store the cut-short segment ffmpeg flushes on the way out before the worker sees ffmpeg exit, and only the exit path applies invariant 40. A viewer would get a freeze or jump of up to about 4 s at that place, as would every viewer of that spec until its segments are swept, and no failure is reported. DOMAINS.md invariant 40; PRODUCT.md: seeking and resuming just work; every failure is reported with its reason. D-043.
acceptanceCriteria: Before any fix, on main as it stands after JS-168 and JS-173, under CI's shape (ffmpeg 6.1, two CPUs no other run is using, a fresh database each run), each cut-read subtest of internal/transcode/recovery_integration_test.go is run 20 times: the three of TestAFailureThatIsNotTheFilesIsMadeAgainForTheRequestThatWaited (a re-encode, a copy, a burn-in) and the one of TestACauseThatPersistsStartsAtMostThreeFreshJobsAndThenFails. The runs and failures of each are recorded in docs/testing.md with each failure's message.

For the waiting-request case, the record says what the 24 bytes are (which MP4 boxes, and whether they hold any frame), which path stored or answered them (the worker's periodic upload check, its exit path, or something else), and whether the cause is this task's (a cut-short segment stored before the exit is seen) or another.

A check with real ffmpeg, under CI's shape, forces this order: ffmpeg has put its cut-short last segment in place and is held before it exits, and the worker's upload check then runs. The check asserts that the order really happened (an upload check ran while the cut segment was in place and ffmpeg was still alive), so a hold that silently misses cannot pass. On today's code it fails because that segment is stored. If it cannot be made to fail, nothing is built: the sighting's verdict returns to cause unknown and the product owner is told.

After the fix, in that order and in the opposite one (the exit seen before the next upload check), no segment shorter than its place is stored for the spec, and none is served to the waiting request or to a later request from another viewer through another stream replica. This holds for each of 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 combinations: the cut at segment 0 and at a segment at least 2 into the film; a re-encode and a copied stream; a source read that fails for good and a file that ends early; a cut that leaves the place with no frame and one that leaves about half of it.

In those same runs, every whole segment made before the cut (at least two in the later-segment case) is stored exactly once and served with its full length, and the place where the cut fell and every place after it have no stored object when the job ends.

The film's true last segment is still stored and served in both orders, for a re-encode and a copy: the playlist's last segment, within 1.5 s of the playlist's length for it. A last segment more than 1.5 s short is still refused, as invariant 40 says.

With ffmpeg held just after it has put a whole segment in place (not at its exit), that segment is stored and served while ffmpeg is held. A fix that keeps every segment back until the next one is made or ffmpeg exits fails this.

A file that ends early: the waiting request gets the failure "the input ended early". Exactly one job runs, with no fresh job within failureMemory, and PlaybackInfo (Jobs.Unavailable) refuses the spec with the memory of that failure.

A source read that fails for good: the waiting request gets the failure that names the source store, not "the input ended early", after at most three fresh jobs (at most four jobs in all), and every one of those jobs ends failed.

Each failed job above is logged with its reason and counted once in jellyscale_transcode_jobs_ended_total{result="failed"}. A job that failed in the forced order is counted as failed, never done or interrupted.

Recorded with ids and counts only (no title or path), stating the window of logs read: how many dogfood jobs failed on an early input end or a source read, and how many of those stored a segment at the place where they stopped, or that the logs cannot tell. If any stored one, the product owner gets a brief on the segments already stored before any purge is built.

Start of play and seek on a healthy film are measured before and after the fix: the time to first segment for a re-encode and a copy, at segment 0 and at a seek, at least 10 runs each on the same pinned shape. The figures are logged and recorded as a record, not a bar (docs/testing.md, Mechanisms not speeds). If the after median is above the before median by more than the spread of the before runs, that goes to the lead as a finding.

No product code changes to fit a check, and nothing is retried or skipped. These stay as they are: the 100 ms upload poll, maxRestarts (3), failureMemory, recoveryWait, the stall limit, the 1.5 s last-segment bound, and every existing check's waits.

DOMAINS.md invariant 40 says the guarantee holds on every path that stores a segment: while ffmpeg runs and at its exit, for a re-encode and for a copy (and so for the encodes that share the copy's path). docs/testing.md's JS-155 row for this sighting carries its new verdict and runs, and docs/status.md is updated if it speaks of it.

No other viewer-visible change: a healthy film played to its end as a re-encode and as a copy stores every segment of its playlist exactly once and no job fails. The existing checks of internal/transcode and internal/api pass unamended.

If the waiting-request case has another cause, nothing is built for it here. It returns to the product owner as a brief with what a viewer would see (a broken segment, a stated failure, or a retry), and JS-159 finishes without it.

After the fix, the persisting-cause subtest passes 20 of 20 under CI's shape: the failure names the source store after at most three fresh jobs, with no segment stored for its place. If the waiting-request case's cause is this task's, its three cut-read subtests also pass 20 of 20, each answered with a whole segment (over 1000 bytes, frames for its full place) made by a fresh job. No check is amended, retried, skipped or given a longer wait.

userStories.title: A worker learns what it holds from the jobs it runs; the operator declares no capacity, and a film is never admitted to stall on a worker that overstates itself
userStories.description: JS-166 measured that declared capacity fails operators: the dogfood's i5-6500 worker declares 3, below a 4K job's 3.2, so it can never help (a helper needs the full price); the 12-thread worker declares 3.5 under a CPU limit of 8, was throttled in 93% of periods and ran the job at about 1.0x; and an operator cannot know a CPU's speed against the reference machine. D-062's start-up benchmark failed on a busy host. D-064: a worker learns what it holds from the jobs it runs, price times measured speed, starting from its processors with a container CPU limit counted, lowered when jobs run under the 1.2x admission bound and raised slowly with margin, smoothed over minutes; transcodeCores becomes an optional ceiling. BL-259's bars are criteria 2 to 4.
acceptanceCriteria: Step, done before Spec and recorded in docs/transcoding.md: a design review built on JS-166's kept job speeds (median 0.97 at limit 8; 1.285 and 1.36 at limit 12), never on the 93% throttling reading, which was not kept (D-067). The review states: the unit and the share; what lowers the figure, what must not (a slow source read, a slow store upload, paused time), and how each is told apart; what the first viewer on an overstated worker gets, and for how long; whether a figure learned on one price row holds for the others; the smoothing window and the margin; the time to converge, and the time to rise again; the recovery schedule, with the most plays the first day can admit above the figure; which way the figure moves during the worker's own extraction; what a worker that cannot read the kernel's CPU figures learns. Each unverified leaf gets a check or returns as a brief. Whether an idle worker helps, and whether the figure survives a restart, belong to JS-178 (D-066). The record also states the longest a worker can run jobs with every sample void because of its own extractions (chapter pictures after a scan, a whole-film read from a network store), and what a play on a worker that still overstates itself gets during it. If that is longer than 10 minutes, a figure not yet learned is still lowered beside an extraction, or it returns as a brief. D-066's condition 3 is decided by D-070.

Step, done before Spec and recorded: the pre-Spec measurement, with its added row: the throttled worker's 4K HDR job with and without an image-track extraction beside it. Any of these returns the task as a brief (D-064, D-066): one learned figure fails to hold across price rows by more than a fifth; the figure cannot be told apart from a slow store; the 4K job runs under 1.0x beside an extraction (a brief against JS-141 and BL-234).

Nothing to declare: an undeclared worker registers at once and starts no ffmpeg of its own, not at start and not later to raise or lower its figure. D-062's 9 cmd/jellyscale tests pass unamended in a 4-process run on 4 pinned CPUs.
An undeclared worker begins from the processors it may use, never more than today's count. A container CPU limit counts as written: a 3.5 limit starts at 3.5, not 4.

A job that runs under 1.2x leaves the figure unchanged when the cause is not the CPU. Each cause is checked: a slowed source read, on POSIX and on S3; a slowed store upload; time spent paused at its lead.

Convergence: take a lone undeclared worker throttled to the i5-6500's speed. Within the stated time of its first 4K HDR job being claimed, its figure comes within a fifth of what it holds (the job's price times that worker's measured speed, over 1.2). Lowering the figure ends no running job.

After convergence, a 4K HDR play on that lone worker is refused at PlaybackInfo within seconds, with no job queued: jellyfin-web shows its "cannot be played at this time" dialog; the log and the JS-153 decision line give the job's cost and the learned capacity; this holds for every ask until a timed rise is due on the stated schedule; a play the worker holds (the 0.8 row) is still admitted.

Within the stated time of a move, every api and stream replica (one of the release before included) and every claim count the figure the worker learned. Each worker's figure is its own: an unthrottled worker beside a throttled one keeps its start figure. A move writes only the worker's own row, and never restores a row the reaper deleted (invariant 25).

The unit and the share (D-066): capacity is the price a worker keeps at 1.2 times real time. A play no one worker holds is admitted shared when two workers each have 0.65 of its price free, for learned and declared workers alike, and refused when either has less. Two undeclared workers throttled to the i5-6500's speed are, once converged, admitted the 4K HDR job shared, and play it within JS-168's bound. No price changes. JS-161's checks stand unamended, except those that state the share as 0.78 of declared cores; those are re-read at 0.65, citing D-066.

A neighbour's short busy moment refuses nothing: on 4 test processes and 4 CPUs, a burst of the stated short length moves the figure by no more than the stated margin and refuses no play the worker holds. After a longer burst lowers the figure, the figure rises again within the stated time of the load dropping. A sample taken while the worker's own extraction runs neither lowers nor raises a learned figure (D-070). That changes only what is learned: a job slowed beside an extraction still asks for a helper as any slow job does (invariant 58), and the existing helper checks pass unamended.

A lowered figure rises from evidence with no wait: any job that shows the worker holds more raises it within the stated sample time, a shared play's own job included. It rises by time only while no job has tested it, and never while running jobs confirm the lowered figure.

Timed-rise backoff, checked on a lone worker throttled to the i5-6500's speed and asked for the 4K HDR job repeatedly: a timed rise that the next job shows wrong at least doubles the gap before the next play admitted above the figure, with no cap under 24 hours; a rise that a job confirms resets the gap; each play admitted above the figure lowers it again within the stated time.

transcodeCores becomes an optional ceiling, listed under Changed guarantees citing D-064: the start figure is the lesser of the processor count and the ceiling; a learned or risen figure never exceeds it; a declared worker still learns below it; a declared figure above the processors no longer counts as written. transcodeSlots is untouched by this task.

The operator can see it and act: at start and on every change, /metrics and the log give the capacity exactly as admission counts it, with its source (assumed, learned or ceiling); a move of more than a fifth from the figure last logged is logged once, with the figure before and after, and a smaller move is not logged; the unhelped line and its counted reason name the source; a worker that cannot read the kernel's CPU figures says so once at start, in the log and on /metrics.
Each failed timed rise is logged with the figure before and after. From the second failed rise since the last confirmed one, the line also names transcodeCores as the ceiling that ends the retries.

Docs, judged by reviewers: docs/running.md gains "Sizing workers", with: requests equal to limits, in whole cores; the CPUs already measured against the price rows; what to do about refusals because cores are short, and about counts of slow jobs that got no helper; a whole node for a 4K-capable worker; what learning cannot see (the worker's own extractions beside a transcode: 16% to 18% slower under a CPU limit for as long as the extraction runs, on a synthetic film, and 0.85x to about 0.6x in the dogfood's one sighting; a whole-film read from a network store runs minutes, up to the hour, once per file version; a second worker with room keeps such a play at real time and a lone worker has none; contention the kernel does not show); what a lone slow worker's timed rise costs a viewer; transcodeCores in the new unit (the i5-6500 at about 2.2 to 2.3, computed); nothing from the 93% reading. A re-encode under 1.0x while its worker's own extraction runs is counted under the slow-job reasons with a reason of its own and logged once per job. docs/status.md lists it under Known gaps citing D-070, with JS-141 as what is planned.

Docs, judged by reviewers: docs/transcoding.md, docs/running.md, docs/status.md's gap line and DOMAINS.md invariant 58 give the share as 0.65 of the price free, with its measured meaning: each of two workers making the job alone at 0.78 of real time. The change for a declared pair is listed under Changed guarantees citing D-066.

userStories.title: A user id in a request names the caller, or the request is refused
userStories.description: About twenty routes take a user id, in the path of the aliases jellyfin-web calls or in a userId query, and ignore it: the answer is the caller's data whatever the id says (routes.go:121, items.go:67). Nothing leaks, but an administrator who asks for another user's list is given their own under the other's name, and no test would notice a handler that started to honour the id without a check. Two handlers that do honour it carry two hand-written copies of the check, in two orders (sessions.go:346-372, user_configuration.go:160-175). This task makes one rule, in one place, before any handler runs.
acceptanceCriteria: Observed first, the main matrix: compat/captures/user-scope-12.4.md and .json record what jellyfin/jellyfin:12.4 does for every route in compat/endpoints.yaml, with an administrator and two non-administrators A and B, each holding data that tells them apart (a favourite, a played item, display preferences, a Configuration, a session). For each route: the status and whose data came back or changed (A, B, the administrator, nobody, or "not a Jellyfin route").

The cases in that matrix: A names B in the {userId} path segment; A names B as userId in the query; A names an id that is no user; A names a malformed id; A names its own id dashed and in upper case; the administrator names B, an id that is no user, and a malformed id; the all-zero id is named.
The capture also records POST /Items/{itemId}/PlaybackInfo with UserId in its body, and GET /Sessions with controllableByUserId, for the same callers and ids.

A script under test/differential/ (capture_user_scope.py, after capture_access.py and capture_user_configuration.py) makes the capture and can be run again from the repository root; the /jellyscale/v1/ routes are recorded as not a Jellyfin route.

Route has Users: 'own' (the default) or 'admin-any'. 'admin-any' is exactly GET /Users/{userId}, POST /Users/Configuration, POST /Users/{userId}/Configuration and POST /UserItems/{itemId}/UserData; every other viewer route is 'own'.

--print-routes writes user: on every route that is not 'anyone' and on no 'anyone' route; compat/endpoints.yaml is regenerated, and docs/access.md's Scope column agrees with Users for every route (by review, not by a test).

On every 'own' route one guard, before the handler, answers 403 when any of these names anyone but the caller: the {userId} path segment; any userId query value; any controllableByUserId query value; UserId in the body of POST /Items/{itemId}/PlaybackInfo or POST /jellyscale/v1/items/{itemId}/playback-info. It holds for a non-administrator and an administrator alike.
On 'own' routes the 403 has the same status and body whether the id is another user's, nobody's or malformed.

Every value counts: ?userId=<A>&userId=<B>, ?userId=<A>&UserId=<B>, A's id in the path with B's in the query, and A's id in the query with B's in the PlaybackInfo body all answer 403, and the guard does not use up PlaybackInfo's body before the handler reads it.

A refused request does nothing: it sends Postgres no statement beyond the token lookup and changes no row of B's or of the caller's. After POST /Sessions/Logout?userId=<B> A's token still works; after POST /UserPlayedItems/{id}?userId=<B> A's played state is unchanged; after DELETE /Videos/ActiveEncodings?userId=<B> A's job is still running; GET /socket?userId=<B> gets no 101.

The caller's own id, dashed or compact, lower or upper case, in any of the four places, answers exactly as the request without it (same status and body); a PlaybackInfo whose body has A's UserId and a profile that forces a transcode gets the same transcode as without it; an empty userId= counts as no id.
Authentication comes first: a request naming B with no token or an unknown token gets 401 unauthorized, never 403.
The guard holds on a process with the api role alone, the stream role alone, and both.

While Postgres is away, on a snapshot route, a request naming B is never served from the snapshot, a request with no user id is served from it as today, and no request is answered 4xx because Postgres is away (invariant 37).
On an 'admin-any' route a non-administrator naming another user's id, or a well-formed id of nobody, gets 403 with the same status and body, and no statement beyond the token lookup is sent.
On an 'admin-any' route a malformed id gets 400 whoever asks, including GET /Users/{malformed} and GET /Users/Configuration, which the {userId} pattern matches.

On an 'admin-any' route an administrator naming a user acts on that user only: GET /Users/{B} returns B's record; a Configuration write naming B changes B's row and none of the administrator's; a UserData write naming B does the same.
On an 'admin-any' route an administrator naming a well-formed id of nobody gets 404 and nothing is written.

Where the path and the query of one 'admin-any' request name different users, a non-administrator gets 403 as for any other user's id, and an administrator gets 400 and nothing is read or written (the lead's addition; Jellyfin's behaviour in the capture is recorded, and it is a difference named in docs/access.md if it differs).
One helper makes the 'admin-any' decision: getUser (users.go), userDataTarget (sessions.go) and saveConfiguration (user_configuration.go) hold no copy of the check.

TestAccess makes A, B and an administrator by SQL and asks every viewer route with B's id in every place the route can take one (path where it has {userId}; userId and controllableByUserId in the query on every route; the body of the two PlaybackInfo POSTs): with A's token 403 on every route; with the administrator's token 403 on every 'own' route; on each of the three handlers of criterion 13.
With the administrator's token and B's id, GET /Users/{B} returns B's record and each of the three admin-any writes lands on B.
After A's sweep and the administrator's sweep of the 'own' routes, every row of B's is byte for byte what it was: users, user_item_data, display_preferences, sessions, devices and session_sockets.

Every 'anyone' route asked with userId=<B>, with no token and with A's token, answers as without the id; POST /Users/AuthenticateByName?userId=<B> with A's name and password signs in A (User.Id is A's).

Named mutants, each failing every run, each shown once by hand in the Spec step and recorded (D-069), none committed: the guard reads the path and not the query; the guard lets an administrator through on an 'own' route; the helper looks the user up before it refuses a non-administrator (as saveConfiguration does today); the guard reads only the first userId value; the guard compares a query id with its letter case.

The JS-116 replay: exactly one case changes and the pull request names it. A non-administrator naming an id that is no user on the three Configuration routes got 404, as on Jellyfin, and now gets 403 so the answer no longer says whether the id is a user. expectedOf in cmd/jellyscale/user_configuration_integration_test.go and the capture file's 'What the replay holds jellyscale to' are amended for that case alone, citing D-075 (the lead's record of the owner's access decision of 2026-11-16). Every other case passes unchanged.

Changed answers listed in the pull request: a request naming another user's id got 200 with the caller's data and now gets 403 (internal/api/playback_integration_test.go lines 657 to 700, which send /Users/{other}/PlayedItems and FavoriteItems and expect the caller's data, are corrected by the lead); GET /Users/{malformed} got 403 or 404 and now gets 400. Neither is visible to a viewer using a client, which sends its own id.

The all-zero id is refused (403 on 'own' routes) as 'not the caller's'. If the capture shows Jellyfin serving it and the capture of a supported client shows it sending one, that returns to the product owner as a trade-off brief, not a quiet relaxation.
jellyfin-web still works: the e2e tier passes unchanged and the differential tier passes with no new entry.

The docs say the new rule: DOMAINS.md invariant 49 and the routes.go comment 'These act on the caller whatever userId says'; docs/access.md line 15 and line 33 (which says a test holds its table to the capture, and none does); docs/api.md lines 7 and 48 (which say the namespace ignores userId); and, under 'Stricter than Jellyfin' in docs/access.md, a row saying an administrator is served another user's view on four routes only, citing the capture entry that shows Jellyfin serving it everywhere.
